sections.title: Security Concepts
sections.content:
INFORMATION SECURITY (INFOSEC)
Information security (infosec) — protection of data resources from unauthorized access, attack, theft, or damage.
CIA Triad (also called AIC, to avoid confusion with the Central Intelligence Agency):
Property | Meaning
Confidentiality | Information can only be read by people explicitly authorized to access it
Integrity | Data is stored/transferred as intended; any modification is authorized
Availability | Information is readily accessible to those authorized to view/modify it
Non-repudiation — a person cannot deny having done something (creating, modifying, sending a resource). Example: a witnessed legal document (a will) provides evidence it was correctly executed.
CYBERSECURITY FRAMEWORK (NIST)
Cybersecurity = provisioning secure processing hardware/software (a subset of infosec). NIST's five functions:
Function | Description
Identify | Develop security policies/capabilities; evaluate risks, threats, vulnerabilities; recommend controls
Protect | Procure/develop, install, operate, decommission IT assets with security embedded at every lifecycle stage
Detect | Ongoing, proactive monitoring that controls remain effective against new threats
Respond | Identify, analyze, contain, eradicate threats to systems/data
Recover | Implement resilience to restore systems/data when other controls fail to prevent attacks
NIST's is just one example of a cybersecurity framework (CSF) — there are many others.
GAP ANALYSIS
• Each security function has associated goals/outcomes, achieved via security controls.
• Gap analysis — a process identifying how an organization's security systems deviate from those required/recommended by a framework.
• Performed when first adopting a framework, when meeting new compliance requirements, or periodically to validate changes.
• Output: overall score per framework section, list of missing/poorly configured controls, remediation recommendations.
• Often involves third-party consultants (specialist knowledge, external oversight, awareness of new trends).
ACCESS CONTROL AND IAM
Access control — governs how subjects/principals (people, devices, software processes) interact with objects (resources: network, server, database, app, file).
Identity and Access Management (IAM) — four processes:
Process | Function
Identification | Creating an account/ID uniquely representing the user, device, or process
Authentication | Proving a subject is who/what it claims to be (via an authentication factor, e.g., password, digital certificate)
Authorization | Determining and enforcing what rights a subject has on a resource, per an authorization model (discretionary = object owner allocates rights; mandatory = rights are system-enforced, unchangeable by users)
Accounting | Tracking authorized usage/rights use; alerting on unauthorized use
Collectively the servers/protocols implementing these are called AAA (authentication, authorization, accounting). These processes apply to both people and systems (e.g., a server must also authenticate itself to clients).

sections.title: Security Controls
sections.content:
SECURITY CONTROL CATEGORIES
A security control gives a system/data asset the properties of confidentiality, integrity, availability, and non-repudiation.
Category | Description | Examples
Managerial | Gives oversight of the information system | Risk identification, tools for evaluating/selecting other controls
Operational | Implemented primarily by people | Security guards, training programs
Technical | Implemented as hardware/software/firmware | Firewalls, antivirus, OS access control models
Physical | Deters/detects physical access to premises/hardware | Alarms, gateways, locks, lighting, cameras
NIST uses a different classification scheme (SP 800-53) — be aware it exists but this course uses the four categories above.
SECURITY CONTROL FUNCTIONAL TYPES
Type | When it Operates | Description | Example
Preventive | Before an attack | Eliminates/reduces likelihood an attack succeeds | Firewall ACLs, antimalware blocking execution
Detective | During an attack | Identifies/records an attempted or successful intrusion | Logs
Corrective | After an attack | Eliminates/reduces impact of a policy violation | Backup restore, patch management
Directive | N/A | Enforces a rule of behavior (policy, SOP, standard) | Employee contract disciplinary clauses, training/awareness programs
Deterrent | N/A | Psychologically discourages an attacker (doesn't physically/logically prevent) | Warning signs of legal penalties
Compensating | N/A | Substitute for a principal/recommended control, same or better protection via different method | Isolating an unsupported system instead of patching it
SECURITY POLICY
A security policy is a formalized statement of how security will be implemented within an organization, protecting the CIA triad. An organization with documented policies and framework-based controls has a strong security posture.
INFORMATION SECURITY ROLES AND RESPONSIBILITIES
Role | Responsibility
CIO (Chief Information Officer) | Overall responsibility for IT function; may also own security
CTO (Chief Technology Officer) | Effective use of new/emerging IT products to achieve business goals
CSO / CISO (Chief Security/Information Security Officer) | Runs a dedicated security department in larger orgs
Managers | Responsibility for a domain (e.g., building control, web services, accounting)
Technical/specialist staff (e.g., ISSO — Information Systems Security Officer) | Implement, maintain, monitor policy
Nontechnical staff | Comply with policy and relevant legislation
Directors/owners | External/legal responsibility (due care, liability)
NIST's NICE (National Initiative for Cybersecurity Education) framework categorizes cybersecurity job tasks and roles.
Typical information security competencies:
• Participate in risk assessments and security testing
• Specify, source, install, configure secure devices/software
• Set up/maintain document access control and user privilege profiles
• Monitor audit logs, review user privileges and access controls
• Manage security incident response and reporting
• Create/test business continuity and disaster recovery plans
• Participate in security training/education
INFORMATION SECURITY BUSINESS UNITS
Unit | Function
SOC (Security Operations Center) | Location where security professionals monitor/protect critical info assets across business functions; typically only feasible for larger orgs (cost/complexity to establish and maintain)
DevSecOps | Extends DevOps (developer/operations collaboration culture) to embed security specialists at every stage of development/deployment — "shift left" (security considered during requirements/planning, not bolted on at the end)
CIRT / CSIRT / CERT (Computer [Security] Incident Response Team / Computer Emergency Response Team) | Single point of contact for notification of security incidents; may sit under the SOC or stand alone

sections.title: Key Takeaways
sections.content:
• Create a security mission statement and supporting policies emphasizing the CIA triad (confidentiality, integrity, availability).
• Assign roles so security tasks/responsibilities are clearly understood and impacts are assessed and mitigated across the organization.
• Consider creating business units/departments/projects to support the security function (SOC, CIRT, DevSecOps).
• Identify and assess laws and industry regulations that impose compliance requirements on the business.
• Select a framework that meets the organization's compliance requirements and business needs.
• Create a matrix of currently deployed security controls (by category and function); consider additional controls for unmatched capabilities.
• Perform a gap analysis against framework requirements to identify goals for developing cybersecurity competencies and improving overall information security assurance.

concept_cards.hook: Centralized platform verifying identity, assigning permissions, and logging actions for an audit trail.
In zero trust architecture, functions defining policy and access decisions.

practice_questions.q: An attacker modifies the amount on a wire transfer while it is in transit. Which part of the CIA triad was violated?
practice_questions.explanation: Unauthorized modification of data is an integrity failure.

practice_questions.q: A company installs bollards in front of its data center entrance to stop vehicles from ramming the doors. Which control category does this represent?
practice_questions.explanation: Bollards are tangible barriers, so they are physical controls.

practice_questions.q: A sender digitally signs a contract so they cannot later deny having sent it. Which concept does this provide?
practice_questions.explanation: A digital signature ties the message to the signer's private key, preventing denial.

practice_questions.q: An organization writes a policy requiring annual risk assessments for every business unit. Which control category is this?
practice_questions.explanation: Managerial controls are policies and oversight decisions that govern how security is run.

practice_questions.q: In the AAA framework, which step decides what a user is allowed to do after they log in?
practice_questions.explanation: Authorization grants permissions after identity is proven.

practice_questions.q: A security team reviews firewall logs every morning to spot unauthorized connection attempts after they happen. Which control type is this?
practice_questions.explanation: Reviewing logs identifies events that already occurred, which is a detective function.

practice_questions.q: Which element of the AAA framework records what a user did during a session?
practice_questions.explanation: Accounting tracks and logs user activity.

practice_questions.q: After ransomware encrypts a file server, the team restores the data from last night's backup. Which control type did the backup provide?
practice_questions.explanation: Corrective controls fix or restore systems after an incident.

practice_questions.q: In a Zero Trust architecture, which component makes the decision to allow or deny an access request?
practice_questions.explanation: The policy engine (part of the control plane) decides; the enforcement point carries the decision out.

practice_questions.q: A legacy application cannot support multifactor authentication, so the team places it on an isolated VLAN with strict ACLs instead. What kind of control is the isolation?
practice_questions.explanation: A compensating control substitutes for a control that cannot be implemented directly.
